newsitem.title: INDIA: India's Congress party keeps heat on Deve Gowda.
newsitem.headline: India's Congress party keeps heat on Deve Gowda.

text.p: India's Congress party, holding the balance of power in a hung parliament, warned Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda on Monday against ignoring its interests, but said it had no immediate plans to pull down his government.

The scandal-plagued party also decided that senior leaders of its decision-making Congress Working Committee (CWC) would disclose their financial assets shortly to spruce up the party's image tarnished by a string of corruption cases.

"The meeting of the CWC notes with concern certain developments which have taken place since the United Front came to power in June," a CWC resolution said after a day-long meeting with Congress President Sitaram Kesri.
"The developments of the past five months have raised a number of questions in the minds of Congress rank and file by the actions and utterances of the United Front leaders," it said.
"Congress calls upon the United Front to change its attitude and instead of hurling abuses at the Congress, take corrective steps...CWC will continue to review the situation as and when it develops."

The resolution also criticised the United Front for what it called poor economic management and blamed the coalition for failing to win a vote for a place on the United Nations' Security Council last month.
Kesri has had several meetings with Deve Gowda to ease ties with the ruling centre-left alliance.
But party officials said these had not prevented some senior Congress members from demanding a withdrawal of support for the 13-group coalition.
The main issue centres on their support for rival candidates for the chief minister's job in the populous state of Uttar Pradesh where local polls returned a hung assembly last month.
Party officials said Kesri had pursuaded several members who urged the Congress to withdraw support to Deve Gowda's five month-old government not to press their demands.

The Congress suffered its worst defeat in this year's general elections, widely seen to be linked to a string of corruption scandals involving charges against former Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao and his cabinet colleagues.
Kesri replaced Rao as Congress president in September after the former prime minister was named in a cheating case.
Rao has been charged in two cases of forgery and bribery. His lawyers have denied the charges. A court will decide on Tuesday whether to extend Rao's pre-emptive bail against arrest.

Deve Gowda formed his coalition in June with decisive support from the Congress after inconclusive general elections in April and May gave his group just 115 seats in the 545-member lower house of parliament.
Congress, despite its worst ever defeat in a general election, won 142 seats. The party has ruled India most of the time since independence from Britain in 1947.

Congress originally supported the United Front to keep out of national power the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), which emerged from the general elections as the single largest party in parliament with 160 seats.
